§11.1.4 Values and Tolerances

📄 Page rule — applied from the page alone

charts-values-and-tolerances · charts values

✅ Normative

Each cell of a chart table holds one of three values. A value printed on the chart MUST be copied character for character and in full. A value not printed MUST be estimated at the mark's visual centre against the mark's own axis. A mark drawn at the baseline, or a labeled position with no mark, MUST be 0.

Printed values — copied exactly

Whatever the chart prints at, on or beside the mark is the value, in full:

  • 25 (13.0%) stays 25 (13.0%) — not 25, not 13.0%, and never 25 countries (13.0%);
  • printed formats stay: thousands separators (11,270), decimal commas (2,08), currency and percent marks, parentheses for negatives (($60B)), footnote markers (<sup>1,2</sup>3.60);
  • printed beats geometry: where the label says 43, the value is 43 even if the bar top measures a hair lower.

Estimated values — the visual centre

Where nothing is printed, the value is read at the mark's visual centre against its own axis — a second axis where the series is scaled by one (see Dual-Axis and Combo Charts§11.2.2), the decade bands of a logarithmic axis (see Log Scale Charts§11.2.6), and a stacked segment's own two boundaries (see Stacked Bars and Waterfalls§11.2.9).

An estimate SHOULD be a value a careful reader could defend within the readability tolerance below — neither falsely precise nor coarser than the axis allows.

How an estimated value is written. An estimated value MUST be written as a bare number in the axis's own format — its unit mark (2.5% on a percent axis) and its digit grouping (17 000 on an axis ticked 18 000) — with no approximation marker, and no more precise than the reading supports: at most one decimal place beyond the axis's tick labels, and two significant figures on a logarithmic axis. Whether a value was printed or estimated is recoverable from the page and is not marked in the Markdown.

Zeros

A mark drawn at the baseline is 0. A labeled position with no mark at all is also 0 — the histogram's empty 1500 bin is 0 (see Bars and Histograms§11.2.1). A stack that simply has no segment of one series leaves that cell empty instead (see Stacked Bars and Waterfalls§11.2.9).

Bars drawn in perspective

A printed bar value is copied first. Otherwise the value-bearing edge is read against the corresponding axis plane, excluding perspective depth. Where the reference plane is ambiguous, the value is the midpoint of the plausible readings.

How a checker compares values

A checker compares each cell with the value it reads off the page:

  • Printed value — the same number, compared exactly. Formatting variants of the same number (thousands separators, decimal comma or point, currency and percent marks) MAY be treated as equal; a different number is wrong.
  • Estimated value — accepted within a relative tolerance of the checker's own reading, chosen by how readable the mark is:
How readable is the mark? Relative tolerance
Sits on a gridline 0.05
Between gridlines, judgeable 0.1
Small, dense, or unclear scale 0.15 – 0.2
Near zero, where a relative band is too narrow wider, as the reading demands (a -1 read on a 10-unit grid takes 0.3)

Most estimates fall between 0.05 and 0.15, and a tolerance above 0.2 is exceptional. The tolerance is the range a careful eye can defend: not so tight that a second careful reading fails it, not so loose that a wrong reading passes. For bars drawn in perspective it is widened to cover every plausible reading.

✅ Sample — health-workforce-2024_p46

One series, twelve bars. Three bars print their number (43, 22, 5) and are copied exactly; the other nine are estimates against the 5-unit grid, most on or near a gridline (tolerance 0.05), the small Software developers bar harder to judge (0.1). Doctors stays 5 although its bar top measures a touch lower. The red EU average bar is an ordinary row: highlighting is styling, not structure. The single series has no printed name, so its column is headed by the value-axis title.

✅ Sample — bars drawn in perspective

Two 3-D bar charts with no printed values. Each bar has a front top edge and a back top edge at different heights. The axis ticks and the baseline sit on the front plane, so the front top edge is the value-bearing edge; every value below is an estimate, read to two significant figures on the first chart and to a tenth of a percent on the second. The tick labels print 1.200 and 12.00%, but an estimate is not written to that precision. The paragraphs between and around the charts are elided.
